title: Values-to-Action Mapping
opening: A value is what matters to you. An activity is one way it might show up. The same value can take different forms, and those forms can ask different things of you.

labels.example: Compare two ways to follow curiosity
labels.exampleContext: These are possible routes, not predictions. Connection asks how the activity expresses curiosity. Possible impact asks what it might change. Personal fit includes your preferences and real constraints.
labels.mapIntro: Write a value in each row, then list more than one activity that could express it. You can save a partial draft; the rows do not submit an assessment.
labels.comparisonIntro: Choose an activity from your map. Note its connection to the value, the effect it could have, whether it fits your circumstances, and what may be difficult. Then name a small, bounded experience that could teach you more. A good fit on paper is a candidate, not a reason to commit a year.
labels.comparisonPlaceholder: Value → activity → connection → possible impact → personal fit → likely difficulty → bounded experience

labels.sourceExcerpt:
Values-to-Action Mapping begins with values. Choose five, generate activities that could express each and compare connection, impact and personal fit. For a promising activity, name its likely difficulty. You now have a particular value–difficulty relationship to test.

The following Passion Crucible passage adds a bounded test: state what an attempt should reveal, set its limits, make the attempt and review what happened. It is a related practice, not a promise that any activity will fit.

reading.title: Read a short guide about a question you already have
reading.connection: You follow curiosity by gathering existing explanations and terms.
reading.impact: It could add background for your next question. Reading alone may not show what you can notice in a nearby setting.
reading.fit: It can be done alone and paused at any point, if a readable source is available.
reading.difficulty: A long or jargon-heavy source can make it hard to find the part that answers your question.
reading.trial: Choose one question, read for up to 10 minutes, then write one detail that sharpened or changed the question. Stop there; no ongoing commitment is implied.

observation.title: Observe birds from a safe, accessible place
observation.connection: You follow curiosity by noticing details before looking for an explanation.
observation.impact: A few notes could make a more specific question visible. They cannot establish a cause or a general pattern.
observation.fit: It can be brief, but it depends on having a safe, accessible place and conditions that work for you.
observation.difficulty: Weather, distance, access or seeing little may interrupt the attempt.
observation.trial: If a safe, accessible place is available, observe for up to 10 minutes. Write three details and one question, then stop. Reading a local guide or looking at a permitted image can be another format if going outside does not fit.
